title: Ἰχώρ
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: After Diomedes’ rush Sthenelus carries out his orders: he holds his own team back, drives off the horses of Aeneas to the Achaean ships and gives them to his comrade Deipylus to take there, and then drives after Diomedes. Diomedes, who knows Aphrodite is a goddess without might and no war-goddess like Athena or Enyo, runs her down through the crowd and wounds her hand with his spear through the robe the Graces made; the immortal blood, ichor, runs, and the poet says why gods have it. She drops her son, Apollo wraps Aeneas in a dark cloud, and Diomedes calls out that she should leave war to others and threatens her with fear of it. Iris leads the wounded goddess out to Ares, who sits on the left of the battle, and Aphrodite begs for his horses and goes with Iris to Olympus. There she falls on the knees of her mother Dione, who asks who has done this, and Aphrodite blames Diomedes and says that the Danaans now fight the gods. Dione tells her to endure, since Ares was bound in a bronze jar by the sons of Aloeus, Hera was shot by the son of Amphitryon, and Hades was shot by the same man and healed by Paieon. She says that Athena set Diomedes on, but that a man who fights the gods does not live to be greeted by his children, and warns that his wife Aegialeia may yet wake her house with her wailing.

sentences.t: ἣ μὲν ἑὸν φίλον υἱὸν ὑπεξέφερεν πολέμοιο·
sentences.tr: hē men heon philon huion hypexepheren polemoio·
sentences.l: She, for her part, her own dear son was bearing out of the war;
sentences.i: She, for her part, was carrying her own dear son out of the war;
sentences.n: ἣ μέν ‘she, for her part’ is Aphrodite, whom the last part left carrying her wounded son Aeneas (the article is a pronoun in Homer, and μέν sets her against Sthenelus, who comes in the next line). ἑὸν φίλον υἱόν is ‘her own dear son’ (ἑός is the possessive ‘own’, not a relative). ὑπεξέφερεν is the imperfect of ὑπεκφέρω ‘carry out from under’, with πολέμοιο, the epic genitive in -οιο, as a genitive of separation: ‘out of the war’. A new paragraph begins at 318.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ υἱὸς Καπανῆος ἐλήθετο συνθεσιάων
τάων ἃς ἐπέτελλε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης,
sentences.tr:
oud’ huios Kapanēos elētheto synthesiaōn
taōn has epetelle boēn agathos Diomēdēs,
sentences.l:
Nor did the son of Capaneus forget the arrangements
that Diomedes, good at the war-cry, enjoined on him,
sentences.i: Nor did the son of Capaneus forget the arrangements that Diomedes, good at the war-cry, had laid upon him,
sentences.n: υἱὸς Καπανῆος ‘the son of Capaneus’ is Sthenelus, whom the Greek does not name here; Καπανῆος has the epic genitive in -ηος. ἐλήθετο is ‘forgot’ and takes the genitive συνθεσιάων ‘arrangements’ (epic genitive plural in -άων), the orders Diomedes gave Sthenelus in the last part (5.260–273). τάων is the article used as a demonstrative, ‘of those’, and ἅς is the relative, object of ἐπέτελλε ‘enjoined’ (ἐπιτέλλω). βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is Diomedes’ stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε τοὺς μὲν ἑοὺς ἠρύκακε μώνυχας ἵππους
νόσφιν ἀπὸ φλοίσβου ἐξ ἄντυγος ἡνία τείνας,
Αἰνείαο δ’ ἐπαΐξας καλλίτριχας ἵππους
ἐξέλασε Τρώων μετ’ ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr:
all’ ho ge tous men heous ērykake mōnychas hippous
nosphin apo phloisbou ex antygos hēnia teinas,
Aineiao d’ epaïxas kallitrichas hippous
exelase Trōōn met’ eÿknēmidas Achaious.
sentences.l:
but he, for his part, held back his own solid-hoofed horses
apart, away from the roar, having stretched the reins from the rail,
and springing upon the fair-maned horses of Aeneas
drove them out from the Trojans among the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.i: but he held back his own solid-hoofed horses, apart from the roar of battle, with the reins made fast to the chariot’s rail, and sprang upon the fair-maned horses of Aeneas and drove them out from the Trojans among the well-greaved Achaeans.
sentences.n: The sentence carries out Diomedes’ orders: τοὺς μὲν ἑοὺς … Αἰνείαο δ’ sets ‘his own horses’ against ‘those of Aeneas’. ἠρύκακε is a reduplicated aorist of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’, and ἑοὺς is again the possessive ‘own’. μώνυχας ‘solid-hoofed’ (with one undivided hoof) is the stock epithet of horses. νόσφιν ἀπὸ φλοίσβου is ‘apart, away from the roar’ (φλοῖσβος is a loud roaring, of surf elsewhere, here of battle; ‘of battle’ in the English is supplied). ἐξ ἄντυγος ἡνία τείνας is ‘having stretched the reins from the rail’, ἄντυξ being the rim of the chariot-body; the sense is that he made them fast there. ἐπαΐξας is the aorist participle of ἐπαΐσσω ‘spring upon’; καλλίτριχας ‘fair-maned’ is the stock epithet of horses (καλλι- ‘fair’ + τρίχες ‘hairs’). ἐξέλασε ‘drove out’ takes the genitive Τρώων ‘from the Trojans’ and μετ’ … Ἀχαιούς ‘among the Achaeans’; ἐϋκνήμιδας ‘well-greaved’ (greaves are shin-guards) is printed with its diaeresis.

sentences.t:
δῶκε δὲ Δηϊπύλῳ ἑτάρῳ φίλῳ, ὃν περὶ πάσης
τῖεν ὁμηλικίης ὅτι οἱ φρεσὶν ἄρτια ᾔδη,
νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν ἐλαυνέμεν·
sentences.tr:
dōke de Dēïpylōi hetarōi philōi, hon peri pasēs
tien homēlikiēs hoti hoi phresin artia ēidē,
nēusin epi glaphyrēisin elaunemen·
sentences.i: and gave them to Deipylus, his dear comrade, whom he honoured above all others of his own age because his mind was fitted to his own, to drive to the hollow ships;
sentences.n: The Greek has no object for δῶκε ‘gave’; Aeneas’ horses, just captured, are understood. Δηϊπύλῳ ἑτάρῳ φίλῳ is the dative ‘to Deipylus, his dear comrade’ (ἑτάρῳ is the epic form of ἑταίρῳ). ὃν περὶ πάσης … ὁμηλικίης is ‘whom beyond all his company of the same age’: περί with the genitive ‘beyond’, and τῖεν is the unaugmented imperfect of τίω ‘honour’. ὅτι οἱ φρεσὶν ἄρτια ᾔδη is ‘because he knew things fitting to him in his mind’: ἄρτια ‘fitting’, ᾔδη the pluperfect of οἶδα (Attic ᾔδει), and the sense is that Deipylus’ thoughts suited Sthenelus’ own. The English of the clause is the one already given to the same words in the Odyssey, which turns ‘knew fitting things’ into ‘his mind was fitted to his own’. νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν ‘to the hollow ships’ has the epic dative plural in -ῃσιν, and ἐλαυνέμεν, with the epic ending -έμεν, is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to drive’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἥρως
ὧν ἵππων ἐπιβὰς ἔλαβ’ ἡνία σιγαλόεντα,
αἶψα δὲ Τυδεΐδην μέθεπε κρατερώνυχας ἵππους
ἐμμεμαώς·
sentences.tr:
autar ho g’ hērōs
hōn hippōn epibas elab’ hēnia sigaloenta,
aipsa de Tydeïdēn methepe kraterōnychas hippous
emmemaōs·
sentences.l:
but he, the hero,
having mounted his own horses, took the glossy reins,
and at once went after Tydeus’-son, driving strong-hoofed horses,
eager;
sentences.i: but the hero mounted his own horses and took the glossy reins, and at once drove his strong-hoofed horses after the son of Tydeus, eager;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἥρως ‘but he, the hero’ is Sthenelus, who now drives his own team. ὧν ἵππων ἐπιβάς is ‘having mounted his own horses’: ὧν is the possessive ‘own’ (genitive plural, agreeing with ἵππων), and ἐπιβάς takes the genitive; the team stands for the chariot it draws. σιγαλόεντα ‘glossy’ is the traditional gloss for the sleek leather of the reins. μέθεπε is the imperfect of μεθέπω ‘go after’ and takes Τυδεΐδην ‘the son of Tydeus’ and, with the sense ‘drive’, κρατερώνυχας ἵππους ‘strong-hoofed horses’ (κρατερός ‘strong’ + ὄνυξ ‘hoof, claw’). ἐμμεμαώς ‘eager’ is the perfect participle of an epic verb meaning ‘strive, be eager’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ Κύπριν ἐπῴχετο νηλέϊ χαλκῷ
γιγνώσκων ὅ τ’ ἄναλκις ἔην θεός, οὐδὲ θεάων
τάων αἵ τ’ ἀνδρῶν πόλεμον κάτα κοιρανέουσιν,
οὔτ’ ἄρ’ Ἀθηναίη οὔτε πτολίπορθος Ἐνυώ.
sentences.tr:
ho de Kyprin epōicheto nēleï chalkōi
gignōskōn ho t’ analkis eēn theos, oude theaōn
taōn hai t’ andrōn polemon kata koiraneousin,
out’ ar’ Athēnaiē oute ptoliporthos Enyō.
sentences.l:
and he went after Cypris with pitiless bronze,
knowing that she was a god without might, and not of the goddesses
those who act as rulers in the war of men,
neither Athena nor city-sacking Enyo.
sentences.i: and he went after Cypris with pitiless bronze, knowing that she was a goddess without might, and not one of those goddesses who act as rulers in the war of men, neither Athena nor Enyo, sacker of cities.
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Diomedes, set against Sthenelus in the last unit. Κύπρις ‘Cypris’ is a name of Aphrodite. ἐπῴχετο is the imperfect of ἐποίχομαι ‘go after’ (the augment and the first vowel have merged), and νηλέϊ χαλκῷ ‘with pitiless bronze’ is his spear. γιγνώσκων ὅ τ’ … ἔην is ‘knowing that she was’: ὅ τε is ‘that’ and ἔην is the epic imperfect of εἰμί. ἄναλκις ‘without might’ (ἀ(ν)- + ἀλκή ‘might’) describes her, and θεός, which is common in gender, is used here of a goddess (the feminine θεά also occurs, as at 405). θεάων τάων αἵ τ’ … κοιρανέουσιν is ‘of those goddesses who act as rulers’ (κοιρανέω, from κοίρανος ‘ruler’), with ἀνδρῶν πόλεμον κάτα ‘in the war of men’ (κάτα is κατά with the accent thrown back). Athena and Enyo, a war-goddess, are the two he has in mind; πτολίπορθος ‘city-sacking’ (πτόλις ‘city’ + πέρθω ‘sack’) is Enyo’s epithet, and Ἀθηναίη is the Ionic form of Athena’s name.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἐκίχανε πολὺν καθ’ ὅμιλον ὀπάζων,
ἔνθ’ ἐπορεξάμενος μεγαθύμου Τυδέος υἱὸς
ἄκρην οὔτασε χεῖρα μετάλμενος ὀξέϊ δουρὶ
ἀβληχρήν·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē rh’ ekichane polyn kath’ homilon opazōn,
enth’ eporexamenos megathymou Tydeos huios
akrēn outase cheira metalmenos oxeï douri
ablēchrēn·
sentences.l:
But when indeed he overtook her, pursuing through the great throng,
then, having stretched out, the son of great-hearted Tydeus
wounded the hand at its end, leaping on with sharp spear,
mild;
sentences.i: But when he overtook her, pursuing her through the great throng, the son of great-hearted Tydeus reached out, leapt on her and wounded her mild hand at its end with his sharp spear;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ‘but when indeed’ opens the time clause: ἐκίχανε ‘overtook’ (κιχάνω) and ὀπάζων ‘pursuing’ (ὀπάζω, ‘make follow’, here ‘press after’) have Diomedes as subject, and πολὺν καθ’ ὅμιλον is ‘through the great throng’. ἐπορεξάμενος ‘having stretched out at her’ and μετάλμενος ‘having leapt upon her’ are aorist participles that describe the lunge; the main verb is οὔτασε ‘wounded’ (οὐτάω), and Τυδέος υἱός is ‘the son of Tydeus’ with the stock epithet μεγαθύμου ‘great-hearted’. ἄκρην … χεῖρα is ‘the hand at its end’, the part beyond the wrist, and ὀξέϊ δουρί ‘with sharp spear’ is the instrument (the diaeresis is printed). ἀβληχρήν, which agrees with χεῖρα, is a word whose meaning is not known; ‘mild’, as in the Odyssey, is a stand-in, and the old guesses are ‘weak’ or ‘tender’. The spot is given exactly in the next unit.

sentences.t:
εἶθαρ δὲ δόρυ χροὸς ἀντετόρησεν
ἀμβροσίου διὰ πέπλου, ὅν οἱ Χάριτες κάμον αὐταί,
πρυμνὸν ὕπερ θέναρος·
sentences.tr:
eithar de dory chroos antetorēsen
ambrosiou dia peplou, hon hoi Charites kamon autai,
prymnon hyper thenaros·
sentences.i: and at once the spear went through the skin, through the ambrosial robe that the Graces themselves had made with toil for her, above the palm, at its base;
sentences.n: εἶθαρ ‘straightway’ is an adverb, and ἀντετόρησεν is the aorist of ἀντιτορέω ‘bore through’, with the genitive χροός ‘the skin’ (χρώς) as what is pierced, and διὰ πέπλου ‘through the robe’ is the next obstacle. ἀμβροσίου is ‘ambrosial’, the stock word for what belongs to gods. ὅν οἱ Χάριτες κάμον αὐταί is ‘which for her the Graces themselves toiled to make’: ὅν is the relative, οἱ ‘for her’ (the enclitic dative pronoun), κάμον the unaugmented aorist of κάμνω ‘toil’, and αὐταί ‘themselves’; the Χάριτες are the Graces. πρυμνὸν ὕπερ θέναρος is ‘at the base, above the palm’: πρυμνόν ‘at the base’, ὕπερ ‘above’ governing the genitive θέναρος, θέναρ being ‘palm’.

sentences.t:
ῥέε δ’ ἄμβροτον αἷμα θεοῖο
ἰχώρ, οἷός πέρ τε ῥέει μακάρεσσι θεοῖσιν·
sentences.tr:
rhee d’ ambroton haima theoio
ichōr, hoios per te rheei makaressi theoisin·
sentences.l:
and flowed the deathless blood of the god,
ichor, such as flows in the blessed gods;
sentences.i: and the goddess’s deathless blood flowed, ichor, such as flows in the blessed gods;
sentences.n: ῥέε is the uncontracted imperfect of ῥέω ‘flow’. ἄμβροτον ‘deathless’ is the house rendering, kept apart from ἀθάνατος ‘immortal’ and ἀμβρόσιος ‘ambrosial’. θεοῖο is the epic genitive in -οιο of θεός, which serves for a goddess as well as a god (the English says ‘goddess’ where the Greek has one in mind). ἰχώρ ‘ichor’ is the word for the fluid that runs in a god’s veins, and it stands in apposition to αἷμα ‘blood’. οἷός πέρ τε ῥέει is ‘such as flows’ (οἷος ‘of the sort that’, πέρ τε emphatic), and μακάρεσσι θεοῖσιν is the epic dative plural, ‘in the blessed gods’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ σῖτον ἔδουσ’, οὐ πίνουσ’ αἴθοπα οἶνον,
τοὔνεκ’ ἀναίμονές εἰσι καὶ ἀθάνατοι καλέονται.
sentences.tr:
ou gar siton edous’, ou pinous’ aithopa oinon,
tounek’ anaimones eisi kai athanatoi kaleontai.
sentences.l:
For they do not eat food, they do not drink the fire-faced wine,
therefore they are bloodless and are called immortal.
sentences.i: For they do not eat food or drink the wine that has the look of fire; that is why they are bloodless and are called immortal.
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ … ‘for … not’ gives the reason the gods’ blood is ichor. ἔδουσ’ is ἔδουσι(ν), the third plural of ἔδω, the epic verb for ἐσθίω ‘eat’, and πίνουσ’ is πίνουσι(ν) ‘drink’, both with the final ι elided. σῖτον ‘food’ is the house rendering of σῖτος. αἴθοπα οἶνον is ‘fire-faced wine’, αἴθοψ being αἴθω ‘burn’ + ὄψ ‘look, face’, with the house rendering ‘that has the look of fire’. τοὔνεκ’ is τούνεκα ‘on that account’. ἀναίμονες ‘bloodless’ (ἀ(ν)- + αἷμα) means without human blood, since the gods have ichor, and ἀθάνατοι ‘immortal’ (ἀ- + θάνατος) is the same sort of negative word; καλέονται is the uncontracted passive of καλέω ‘call’.

sentences.t: ἣ δὲ μέγα ἰάχουσα ἀπὸ ἕο κάββαλεν υἱόν·
sentences.tr: hē de mega iachousa apo heo kabbalen huion·
sentences.l: And she, crying out greatly, threw her son down from herself;
sentences.i: With a great cry she threw her son down from herself;
sentences.n: ἣ δέ ‘and she’ is Aphrodite again. ἰάχουσα is the participle of ἰάχω ‘cry out’, with μέγα ‘greatly’ as its adverb. ἀπὸ ἕο … κάββαλεν is ‘threw down from herself’: ἕο is the epic genitive of the reflexive pronoun, and κάββαλεν stands for κατέβαλεν, the preverb cut short and assimilated before β. The wound has made her let go of Aeneas.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὸν μὲν μετὰ χερσὶν ἐρύσατο Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων
κυανέῃ νεφέλῃ, μή τις Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων
χαλκὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσι βαλὼν ἐκ θυμὸν ἕλοιτο·
sentences.tr:
kai ton men meta chersin erysato Phoibos Apollōn
kyaneēi nephelēi, mē tis Danaōn tachypōlōn
chalkon eni stēthessi balōn ek thymon heloito·
sentences.i: and Phoebus Apollo rescued him, holding him in his hands in a dark cloud, lest any of the Danaans with their swift colts strike bronze into his chest and take his life.
sentences.n: καὶ τὸν μέν ‘and him’ is Aeneas, set against ἣ δέ in the last unit. ἐρύσατο is the aorist middle of ἐρύομαι ‘rescue, protect’, μετὰ χερσίν ‘in his hands’ puts Aeneas in the god’s hands (μετά takes the dative here), and κυανέῃ νεφέλῃ ‘in a dark cloud’ (κυάνεος ‘dark’) hides him; Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων is ‘Phoebus Apollo’. The clause μή τις … ἕλοιτο ‘lest any … take’ repeats the end of the last part, which says the same of Aphrodite’s robe, in the same English: Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων ‘of the Danaans with swift colts’, χαλκὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσι βαλών ‘having cast bronze in his chest’ (bronze stands for the weapon), and ἐκ θυμὸν ἕλοιτο ‘take out his life’ (ἐκ is split from its verb, and θυμός here is the life).

sentences.t: τῇ δ’ ἐπὶ μακρὸν ἄϋσε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: tēi d’ epi makron aÿse boēn agathos Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: And at her he shouted loudly, Diomedes, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: And Diomedes, good at the war-cry, cried out loudly at her:
sentences.n: τῇ δ’ ἐπὶ … ἄϋσε is ‘and … cried out at her’, the preverb ἐπί standing apart from its verb (tmesis), with τῇ ‘her’, the article used as a pronoun in the dative, in front of it and μακρόν between it and the verb; the diaeresis in ἄϋσε keeps α and υ in separate syllables. μακρόν ‘long’ is used as an adverb of voice, ‘loudly’. βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is the stock epithet, translated every time, and here it fits the moment, since he is shouting.

sentences.t: εἶκε Διὸς θύγατερ πολέμου καὶ δηϊοτῆτος·
sentences.tr: eike Dios thygater polemou kai dēïotētos·
sentences.l: “Give way, daughter of Zeus, from war and fighting;
sentences.i: “Withdraw, daughter of Zeus, from war and fighting;
sentences.n: Diomedes speaks to Aphrodite. εἶκε is the imperative of εἴκω ‘give way, yield’, which takes the genitive πολέμου καὶ δηϊοτῆτος ‘from war and fighting’ (δηϊοτής ‘fighting’, genitive δηϊοτῆτος). Διὸς θύγατερ is the vocative ‘daughter of Zeus’, and the edition prints no quotation marks, so the marks in the English are ours.

sentences.t: ἦ οὐχ ἅλις ὅττι γυναῖκας ἀνάλκιδας ἠπεροπεύεις;
sentences.tr: ē ouch halis hotti gynaikas analkidas ēperopeueis;
sentences.l: Is it not enough that you deceive women without might?
sentences.i: Is it not enough that you deceive women without might?
sentences.n: ἦ οὐχ ἅλις ‘is it not enough’ opens a question (the Greek question mark is the semicolon). ὅττι is ὅτι ‘that’ with the epic doubled τ, and ἠπεροπεύεις is ‘you deceive’ (ἠπεροπεύω, ‘beguile, cheat’). γυναῖκας ἀνάλκιδας ‘women without might’ uses the word the poet used of Aphrodite at 331, ἄναλκις, so Diomedes calls her what the poet has called her.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὲ σύ γ’ ἐς πόλεμον πωλήσεαι, ἦ τέ σ’ ὀΐω
ῥιγήσειν πόλεμόν γε καὶ εἴ χ’ ἑτέρωθι πύθηαι.
sentences.tr:
ei de sy g’ es polemon pōlēseai, ē te s’ oïō
rhigēsein polemon ge kai ei ch’ heterōthi pythēai.
sentences.l:
But if you go back and forth into war, truly I suspect you
will shudder at war, even if you learn of it somewhere else.”
sentences.i: But if you go back and forth into war, I truly suspect you will shudder at war, even if you hear of it somewhere else.”
sentences.n: πωλήσεαι is the future middle of πωλέομαι ‘go to and fro’ with the epic ending -εαι (Attic -ῃ), ‘if you go about into war’. ἦ τέ σ’ ὀΐω is ‘truly I suspect you’, ὀΐω being ‘I suspect’, and it takes the future infinitive ῥιγήσειν ‘will shudder’ (ῥιγέω), with πόλεμόν γε ‘at war itself’. καὶ εἴ χ’ is καὶ εἴ κε ‘even if’ (κε is the epic form of ἄν), with the aorist subjunctive πύθηαι, the epic form of πύθῃ, from πυνθάνομαι ‘learn, hear of’; ἑτέρωθι is ‘elsewhere’, with the suffix -θι of place. The threat is that she will shudder at war even at second hand.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, ἣ δ’ ἀλύουσ’ ἀπεβήσετο, τείρετο δ’ αἰνῶς·
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hē d’ alyous’ apebēseto, teireto d’ ainōs·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and she, distraught, went away, and was dreadfully worn down;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and she went away distraught, dreadfully worn down;
sentences.n: A new paragraph begins at 352. ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφατο, with the final vowel elided), closing Diomedes’ speech. ἣ δ’ ‘and she’ is Aphrodite. ἀλύουσ’ is the participle of ἀλύω ‘be beside oneself, be distraught’, and ἀπεβήσετο is an epic aorist of ἀποβαίνω ‘go away’ (Attic ἀπέβη). τείρετο is the imperfect passive of τείρω ‘wear down’, with αἰνῶς ‘dreadfully’ as its adverb.

sentences.t:
τὴν μὲν ἄρ’ Ἶρις ἑλοῦσα ποδήνεμος ἔξαγ’ ὁμίλου
ἀχθομένην ὀδύνῃσι, μελαίνετο δὲ χρόα καλόν.
sentences.tr:
tēn men ar’ Iris helousa podēnemos exag’ homilou
achthomenēn odynēisi, melaineto de chroa kalon.
sentences.l:
Her then wind-footed Iris, having taken her, led out of the throng,
distressed by her pains, and her fair skin was growing dark.
sentences.i: Wind-footed Iris took her and led her out of the throng, distressed by her pains, while her fair skin grew dark.
sentences.n: τὴν μὲν ἄρ’ ‘her then’ is Aphrodite, taken by Ἶρις ‘Iris’, the messenger of the gods, whose stock epithet ποδήνεμος ‘wind-footed’ is translated every time. ἑλοῦσα ‘having taken’ is the aorist participle of αἱρέω, and ἔξαγ’ is ‘led out’ (ἐξάγω), with ὁμίλου, a genitive of separation, ‘out of the throng’. ἀχθομένην ὀδύνῃσι is ‘distressed by pains’ (ἄχθομαι ‘be burdened, vexed’, and ὀδύνῃσι the epic dative plural). μελαίνετο is the imperfect passive of μελαίνω ‘grow dark’, and χρόα καλόν ‘fair skin’ is an accusative of respect, ‘dark as to her fair skin’, which the English turns into a subject.

sentences.t:
εὗρεν ἔπειτα μάχης ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ θοῦρον Ἄρηα
ἥμενον·
sentences.tr:
heuren epeita machēs ep’ aristera thouron Arēa
hēmenon·
sentences.l:
Then she found, on the left of the battle, impetuous Ares
sitting;
sentences.i: Then she found impetuous Ares sitting on the left of the battle;
sentences.n: The subject of εὗρεν ‘found’ is Iris, carried over from the last unit. μάχης ἐπ’ ἀριστερά is ‘on the left of the battle’ (ἀριστερά ‘the left-hand side’ used as a noun, with μάχης the genitive), and θοῦρον Ἄρηα ‘impetuous Ares’ keeps the house rendering of θοῦρος; Ἄρηα is the accusative of Ἄρης, here the god. ἥμενον ‘sitting’ is the participle of ἧμαι, in the accusative to agree with Ἄρηα.

sentences.t: ἠέρι δ’ ἔγχος ἐκέκλιτο καὶ ταχέ’ ἵππω·
sentences.tr: ēeri d’ enchos ekeklito kai tache’ hippō·
sentences.l: and in mist his spear had been propped, and the two swift horses;
sentences.i: his spear was propped in the mist, and his two swift horses too;
sentences.n: ἠέρι is the dative of ἠήρ ‘mist’, ‘in the mist’, a dative of place. ἐκέκλιτο is the pluperfect passive of κλίνω ‘lean’, ‘had been leaned, was propped’, and the one verb serves both ἔγχος ‘spear’ and the dual ταχέ’ ἵππω ‘the two swift horses’ (ταχέε, the dual of ταχύς). The picture is of Ares sitting with spear and team in a mist, and why the mist is there is not said.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ γνὺξ ἐριποῦσα κασιγνήτοιο φίλοιο
πολλὰ λισσομένη χρυσάμπυκας ᾔτεεν ἵππους·
sentences.tr:
hē de gnyx eripousa kasignētoio philoio
polla lissomenē chrysampykas ēiteen hippous·
sentences.l:
and she, having crashed down on her knees, her dear brother
entreating much, asked for the gold-frontleted horses:
sentences.i: and she crashed down on her knees before her dear brother and, entreating him much, asked for his horses with their golden frontlets:
sentences.n: ἣ δέ ‘and she’ is Aphrodite, and the brother is Ares. γνὺξ ἐριποῦσα is ‘having crashed down on her knees’, ἐριποῦσα being the aorist participle of ἐρείπω, the verb used of Aeneas’ fall. κασιγνήτοιο φίλοιο is the genitive ‘of her dear brother’, which goes best with λισσομένη ‘entreating’ (λίσσομαι), and πολλά ‘much’ is an adverb. χρυσάμπυκας ‘gold-frontleted’ is the stock epithet of horses, from χρυσός ‘gold’ and ἄμπυξ ‘frontlet’, a band worn on the forehead; it is translated the same way each time. ᾔτεεν is the uncontracted imperfect of αἰτέω ‘ask for’.

sentences.t:
φίλε κασίγνητε κόμισαί τέ με δός τέ μοι ἵππους,
ὄφρ’ ἐς Ὄλυμπον ἵκωμαι ἵν’ ἀθανάτων ἕδος ἐστί.
sentences.tr:
phile kasignēte komisai te me dos te moi hippous,
ophr’ es Olympon hikōmai hin’ athanatōn hedos esti.
sentences.l:
“Dear brother, convey me, and give me the horses,
so that I may reach Olympus, where the seat of the immortals is.
sentences.i: “Dear brother, carry me away and give me the horses, so that I may reach Olympus, where the seat of the immortals is.
sentences.n: Aphrodite speaks to Ares. φίλε κασίγνητε is the vocative ‘dear brother’. κόμισαι is the aorist imperative middle of κομίζω ‘convey, take care of’, and δός the aorist imperative of δίδωμι ‘give’; τέ … τέ joins the two commands. ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive ἵκωμαι gives the purpose, ‘so that I may reach’, with ἐς Ὄλυμπον ‘to Olympus’ and ἵν’ ‘where’. ἀθανάτων ἕδος is ‘the seat of the immortals’, ἕδος being ‘seat, abode’. There are no quotation marks in the edition. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the short ι of φίλε must count long in the first foot, the final -τε of κασίγνητε counts long at the start of the third foot, and μοι is shortened before the vowel of ἵππους.

sentences.t:
λίην ἄχθομαι ἕλκος ὅ με βροτὸς οὔτασεν ἀνὴρ
Τυδεΐδης, ὃς νῦν γε καὶ ἂν Διὶ πατρὶ μάχοιτο.
sentences.tr:
liēn achthomai helkos ho me brotos outasen anēr
Tydeïdēs, hos nyn ge kai an Dii patri machoito.
sentences.l:
I am greatly distressed at the wound which a mortal man wounded me with,
Tydeus’-son, who now would fight even with father Zeus.”
sentences.i: I am greatly distressed by the wound that a mortal man dealt me, the son of Tydeus, who by now would fight even with father Zeus.”
sentences.n: λίην ἄχθομαι ‘I am greatly distressed’ takes the accusative ἕλκος ‘wound’, and ὅ is the neuter relative, ‘which’, the object of οὔτασεν together with με, ‘wounded me with a wound’; it can also be read as the conjunction ὅ = ὅτι ‘that’ with nearly the same sense. βροτὸς ἀνήρ is ‘a mortal man’, set in bitter contrast to a goddess, and Τυδεΐδης ‘the son of Tydeus’ follows in apposition. ὃς νῦν γε καὶ ἂν … μάχοιτο is ‘who now would even fight’, a potential optative with ἄν, and Διὶ πατρί is ‘with father Zeus’ (the dative after μάχομαι). She exaggerates.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τῇ δ’ ἄρ’ Ἄρης δῶκε χρυσάμπυκας ἵππους·
sentences.tr: hōs phato, tēi d’ ar’ Arēs dōke chrysampykas hippous·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and to her Ares gave the gold-frontleted horses;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Ares gave her the horses with their golden frontlets;
sentences.n: A new paragraph begins at 363. ὣς φάτο is ‘so she spoke’ (φάτο is the unaugmented ἔφατο), and τῇ is the article as a pronoun in the dative, ‘to her’. Ares answers with the gift alone, the same χρυσάμπυκας ἵππους she asked for at 358, and says nothing.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἐς δίφρον ἔβαινεν ἀκηχεμένη φίλον ἦτορ,
πὰρ δέ οἱ Ἶρις ἔβαινε καὶ ἡνία λάζετο χερσί,
μάστιξεν δ’ ἐλάαν, τὼ δ’ οὐκ ἀέκοντε πετέσθην.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ es diphron ebainen akēchemenē philon ētor,
par de hoi Iris ebaine kai hēnia lazeto chersi,
mastixen d’ elaan, tō d’ ouk aekonte petesthēn.
sentences.l:
And she stepped into the chariot, grieved in her dear heart,
and beside her Iris stepped and took the reins in her hands,
and she whipped them to drive on, and the two, not unwilling, flew.
sentences.i: She got into the chariot, grieved at heart, and Iris got in beside her and took the reins in her hands; she whipped them to drive them on, and the pair flew not unwilling.
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ ‘and she’ is Aphrodite, with ἀκηχεμένη φίλον ἦτορ ‘grieved in her dear heart’, a perfect participle with an accusative of respect. ἔβαινεν is the imperfect of βαίνω ‘step, go’; πὰρ δέ οἱ is παρὰ δέ οἱ ‘and beside her’, and Iris takes the reins (ἡνία), λάζετο being the imperfect of λάζομαι ‘take’ and χερσί an epic dative plural, ‘in her hands’. μάστιξεν δ’ ἐλάαν ‘she whipped them to drive on’ has Iris as subject, ἐλάαν being the infinitive of ἐλαύνω; τώ is the dual article as a pronoun, ‘the two’, i.e. the horses, with the duals ἀέκοντε ‘unwilling’ and πετέσθην ‘they flew’. The last line stands also in the Odyssey, said of Peisistratus driving out of Pylos, and has the same English here.

sentences.t: αἶψα δ’ ἔπειθ’ ἵκοντο θεῶν ἕδος αἰπὺν Ὄλυμπον·
sentences.tr: aipsa d’ epeith’ hikonto theōn hedos aipyn Olympon·
sentences.l: At once then they reached the seat of the gods, steep Olympus;
sentences.i: At once they reached the seat of the gods, steep Olympus;
sentences.n: αἶψα ‘at once’ and ἔπειτα ‘then’ are adverbs, and ἵκοντο is the unaugmented aorist middle of ἱκνέομαι ‘come to, reach’. θεῶν ἕδος is ‘the seat of the gods’, and αἰπὺν Ὄλυμπον ‘steep Olympus’ is in apposition to it, αἰπύς ‘steep’ being the stock epithet of high places.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἵππους ἔστησε ποδήνεμος ὠκέα Ἶρις
λύσασ’ ἐξ ὀχέων, παρὰ δ’ ἀμβρόσιον βάλεν εἶδαρ·
sentences.tr:
enth’ hippous estēse podēnemos ōkea Iris
lysas’ ex ocheōn, para d’ ambrosion balen eidar·
sentences.l:
There the horses made stand wind-footed, swift Iris,
having loosed them from the chariot, and beside them threw ambrosial food;
sentences.i: There Iris, wind-footed and swift, halted the horses and loosed them from the chariot, and threw ambrosial food down beside them;
sentences.n: ἔστησε is the transitive aorist of ἵστημι, ‘made stand, halted’. ποδήνεμος ὠκέα Ἶρις is ‘wind-footed, swift Iris’, the two epithets each translated. λύσασ’ is ‘having loosed’ (λύω), with ἐξ ὀχέων ‘from the chariot’ (ὄχεα is a plural for one chariot). παρὰ … βάλεν is tmesis for ‘threw beside’; εἶδαρ is a rare word for ‘food’, here the horses’ fodder, and ἀμβρόσιον ‘ambrosial’ makes it the food of gods’ horses.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἐν γούνασι πῖπτε Διώνης δῖ’ Ἀφροδίτη
μητρὸς ἑῆς·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ en gounasi pipte Diōnēs di’ Aphroditē
mētros heēs·
sentences.l:
And she, heavenly Aphrodite, fell on the knees of Dione,
her own mother;
sentences.i: and heavenly Aphrodite fell on the knees of Dione, her own mother;
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ ‘and she’ is Aphrodite, named only afterwards as δῖ’ Ἀφροδίτη ‘heavenly Aphrodite’ (δῖος is the stock epithet, translated every time; the final vowel is elided). ἐν γούνασι Διώνης is ‘on the knees of Dione’: γούνασι is the dative plural of γόνυ ‘knee’, and Dione, named here for the first time in this part, is Aphrodite’s mother. μητρὸς ἑῆς is ‘her own mother’, with the possessive ἑός (feminine genitive ἑῆς). πῖπτε is the imperfect of πίπτω ‘fall’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἀγκὰς ἐλάζετο θυγατέρα ἥν,
χειρί τέ μιν κατέρεξεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἐκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ ankas elazeto thygatera hēn,
cheiri te min katerexen epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomaze·
sentences.l:
and she took her own daughter in her arms,
and stroked her with her hand, and spoke a word, and called her by name:
sentences.i: and took her own daughter in her arms, and stroked her with her hand, and spoke, calling her by name:
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ ‘and she’ is now Dione. ἀγκάς ‘in her arms’ is an adverb, and ἐλάζετο is the imperfect of λάζομαι ‘take’. ἥν is the possessive ‘her own’, agreeing with θυγατέρα ‘daughter’, not a relative. χειρί τέ μιν κατέρεξεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἐκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε is the formula of caress and address, with the same English each time; κατέρεξεν is the aorist of καταρρέζω ‘stroke’, and ἐκ … ὀνόμαζε is tmesis for ‘called out by name’, with μιν ‘her’. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: it has only twelve syllables, the least a hexameter can have, so it fits only as six spondees, and short syllables in ἐλάζετο and θυγατέρα have to be counted long.

sentences.t:
τίς νύ σε τοιάδ’ ἔρεξε φίλον τέκος Οὐρανιώνων
μαψιδίως, ὡς εἴ τι κακὸν ῥέζουσαν ἐνωπῇ;
sentences.tr:
tis ny se toiad’ erexe philon tekos Ouraniōnōn
mapsidiōs, hōs ei ti kakon rhezousan enōpēi;
sentences.l:
“Who then of the Uranians has done such things to you, dear child,
without cause, as if you were doing some evil openly?”
sentences.i: “Which of the gods of heaven has done such things to you, dear child, without cause, as if you were doing some evil in the open?”
sentences.n: Dione speaks to Aphrodite. τίς … Οὐρανιώνων is ‘which of the Uranians’: Οὐρανίωνες are the gods of heaven, descendants of Οὐρανός ‘Heaven’, in the genitive plural, with the vocative φίλον τέκος ‘dear child’ set between. νύ is ‘then’, τοιάδ’ is τοιάδε ‘such things’, and ἔρεξε is the aorist of ῥέζω ‘do’. μαψιδίως ‘without cause’ keeps the Odyssey’s rendering. ὡς εἴ τι κακὸν ῥέζουσαν is ‘as if you were doing some evil’, the participle agreeing with σε ‘you’, and ἐνωπῇ is ‘openly, in plain sight’. The question mark is the Greek semicolon.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα φιλομμειδὴς Ἀφροδίτη·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ēmeibet’ epeita philommeidēs Aphroditē·
sentences.l: Her then answered smile-loving Aphrodite:
sentences.i: Then smile-loving Aphrodite answered her:
sentences.n: A new paragraph begins at 375. τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ‘and then answered her’ is the stock opening of a reply (the article is a pronoun, and ἠμείβετο, the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘reply’, is kept as ‘answered’ every time). φιλομμειδής ‘smile-loving’ (φιλο- ‘loving’ + μειδάω ‘smile’, the μ doubled in this spelling) is Aphrodite’s stock epithet, translated every time even though she is hurt.

sentences.t:
οὖτά με Τυδέος υἱὸς ὑπέρθυμος Διομήδης,
οὕνεκ’ ἐγὼ φίλον υἱὸν ὑπεξέφερον πολέμοιο
Αἰνείαν, ὃς ἐμοὶ πάντων πολὺ φίλτατός ἐστιν.
sentences.tr:
outa me Tydeos huios hyperthymos Diomēdēs,
hounek’ egō philon huion hypexepheron polemoio
Aineian, hos emoi pantōn poly philtatos estin.
sentences.l:
“Wounded me did the son of Tydeus, high-spirited Diomedes,
because I was bearing my dear son out of the war,
Aeneas, who is by far the dearest of all to me.
sentences.i: “The son of Tydeus, high-spirited Diomedes, wounded me, because I was carrying my dear son out of the war, Aeneas, who is by far the dearest of all to me.
sentences.n: Aphrodite answers Dione. οὖτά is the short aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound’, third singular, here with με ‘me’ (compare οὔτασε at 336). Τυδέος υἱός has the epic genitive in -εος, and ὑπέρθυμος ‘high-spirited’ is Diomedes’ stock epithet. οὕνεκ’ is οὕνεκα ‘because’, and ὑπεξέφερον is the first-person form of the verb used of her at 318, ‘I was carrying out’, with πολέμοιο ‘out of the war’. Αἰνείαν is in apposition to φίλον υἱόν. ὃς … πάντων πολὺ φίλτατος is ‘who is by far dearest of all’: φίλτατος is the superlative of φίλος, with πάντων a genitive of comparison and πολύ ‘by far’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔτι Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν φύλοπις αἰνή,
ἀλλ’ ἤδη Δαναοί γε καὶ ἀθανάτοισι μάχονται.
sentences.tr:
ou gar eti Trōōn kai Achaiōn phylopis ainē,
all’ ēdē Danaoi ge kai athanatoisi machontai.
sentences.l:
For no longer is it the fearsome battle-din of Trojans and Achaeans,
but already the Danaans fight even with the immortals.”
sentences.i: For it is no longer the fearsome din of battle between Trojans and Achaeans; no, already the Danaans are fighting even with the immortals.”
sentences.n: οὐ γὰρ ἔτι ‘for no longer’ gives her reason for the complaint. The first line has no verb: φύλοπις αἰνή ‘fearsome battle-din’ is the predicate, ‘it is no longer the fearsome battle-din of Trojans and Achaeans’ (the genitives name the two sides). ἀλλ’ ἤδη ‘but already’ turns to the Δαναοί, one of the poem’s three names for the army; the poet’s change from Ἀχαιῶν in one line to Δαναοί in the next is kept in both layers. μάχονται ‘fight’ takes the epic dative ἀθανάτοισι ‘with the immortals’, καί is ‘even’, and γε stresses Δαναοί.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Διώνη, δῖα θεάων·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ēmeibet’ epeita Diōnē, dia theaōn·
sentences.l: Her then answered Dione, heavenly-one of goddesses:
sentences.i: Then Dione, heavenly even among goddesses, answered her:
sentences.n: A new paragraph begins at 381. The reply formula of 375 again, now with Dione as the speaker. δῖα θεάων is ‘heavenly even among goddesses’, δῖα being the stock epithet and θεάων the genitive plural in -άων; the English keeps the Odyssey’s wording.

sentences.t: τέτλαθι τέκνον ἐμόν, καὶ ἀνάσχεο κηδομένη περ·
sentences.tr: tetlathi teknon emon, kai anascheo kēdomenē per·
sentences.l: “Endure, my child, and hold out, grieved though you are;
sentences.i: “Endure it, my child, and bear up, worried as you are;
sentences.n: Dione consoles her daughter. τέτλαθι is the perfect imperative of τλάω ‘endure’, and ἀνάσχεο the aorist imperative middle of ἀνέχομαι ‘hold out, bear up’ (-εο for -ου). The two stand together at 1.586, where Hephaestus says the pair to his mother, and the English is the same, with ‘child’ for ‘mother’. τέκνον ἐμόν is ‘my child’ (ἐμόν is neuter, agreeing with τέκνον), and κηδομένη περ is ‘though troubled’, the participle of κήδομαι ‘be distressed’ agreeing with the feminine ‘you’, with περ ‘though’.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ γὰρ δὴ τλῆμεν Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες
ἐξ ἀνδρῶν χαλέπ’ ἄλγε’ ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισι τιθέντες.
sentences.tr:
polloi gar dē tlēmen Olympia dōmat’ echontes
ex andrōn chalep’ alge’ ep’ allēloisi tithentes.
sentences.l:
for many of us who hold the Olympian halls endured
from men hard pains, laying them on one another.
sentences.i: For many of us who hold the halls of Olympus have endured hard pains at the hands of men, laying them on one another.
sentences.n: γάρ ‘for’ gives the reason for patience: even the gods have suffered. τλῆμεν is the aorist first plural of τλάω ‘endure’, with the accusative ἄλγεα ‘pains’ (here ἄλγε’, elided), χαλεπά ‘hard’. Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες is the stock phrase ‘who hold the Olympian halls’. ἐξ ἀνδρῶν ‘from men’ names the source of the pains, and ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισι τιθέντες ‘laying them on one another’, the participle of τίθημι, is loosely attached, so that the sense is that gods and men trade injuries; the examples that follow show gods hurt by the sons of Aloeus and by the son of Amphitryon.

sentences.t:
τλῆ μὲν Ἄρης ὅτε μιν Ὦτος κρατερός τ’ Ἐφιάλτης
παῖδες Ἀλωῆος, δῆσαν κρατερῷ ἐνὶ δεσμῷ·
sentences.tr:
tlē men Arēs hote min Ōtos krateros t’ Ephialtēs
paides Alōēos, dēsan kraterōi eni desmōi·
sentences.l:
Ares endured, when Otus and strong Ephialtes,
the sons of Aloeus, bound him in a strong bond;
sentences.i: Ares endured it, when Otus and strong Ephialtes, the sons of Aloeus, bound him in a strong bond;
sentences.n: τλῆ μέν ‘Ares endured’ opens a list of three: τλῆ μὲν Ἄρης, then τλῆ δ’ Ἥρη, then τλῆ δ’ Ἀΐδης. τλῆ is the athematic aorist third singular of τλάω ‘endure’. ὅτε μιν ‘when … him’ has Ὦτος and Ἐφιάλτης, Otus and Ephialtes, as subjects, παῖδες Ἀλωῆος ‘the sons of Aloeus’ (the epic genitive in -ηος) in apposition, and κρατερός ‘strong’ the stock epithet of Ephialtes. δῆσαν is the aorist third plural of δέω ‘bind’, and κρατερῷ ἐνὶ δεσμῷ is ‘in a strong bond’, with ἐνί between the adjective and its noun.

sentences.t: χαλκέῳ δ’ ἐν κεράμῳ δέδετο τρισκαίδεκα μῆνας·
sentences.tr: chalkeōi d’ en keramōi dedeto triskaideka mēnas·
sentences.l: in a bronze jar he lay bound for thirteen months;
sentences.i: he lay bound in a bronze jar for thirteen months;
sentences.n: χαλκέῳ … ἐν κεράμῳ is ‘in a bronze jar’: κέραμος is potter’s clay and the jar made of it, and the jar here is bronze, a prison. δέδετο is the pluperfect passive of δέω ‘bind’, ‘had been bound’, taken as ‘lay bound’. τρισκαίδεκα is ‘thirteen’ (‘three and ten’), and μῆνας is the accusative of duration, ‘for months’.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κεν ἔνθ’ ἀπόλοιτο Ἄρης ἆτος πολέμοιο,
εἰ μὴ μητρυιὴ περικαλλὴς Ἠερίβοια
Ἑρμέᾳ ἐξήγγειλεν·
sentences.tr:
kai ny ken enth’ apoloito Arēs atos polemoio,
ei mē mētruiē perikallēs Ēeriboia
Hermeāi exēngeilen·
sentences.i: And now Ares, who never has enough of war, would have perished there, had not their stepmother, the very fair Eeriboea, told Hermes;
sentences.n: καί νύ κεν ἔνθ’ ἀπόλοιτο … εἰ μή ‘and now … would have perished there, if not’ is the same turn as in the last part, where Aeneas was nearly lost. ἆτος πολέμοιο ‘insatiate of war’ (ἆτος ‘insatiable’, with a genitive of the thing) is an old tag for the war-god whose traditional sense is ‘insatiable’. μητρυιή is ‘stepmother’, and the Greek says no more; the context shows she is the stepmother of Otus and Ephialtes, so the English adds ‘their’. Ἠερίβοια is Eeriboea, and περικαλλής ‘very fair’ is the house rendering. Ἑρμέᾳ is the Ionic dative of Hermes, and ἐξήγγειλεν is the aorist of ἐξαγγέλλω ‘report, tell’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἐξέκλεψεν Ἄρηα
ἤδη τειρόμενον, χαλεπὸς δέ ἑ δεσμὸς ἐδάμνα.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ exeklepsen Arēa
ēdē teiromenon, chalepos de he desmos edamna.
sentences.l:
and he stole Ares out, already being worn down,
and the hard bond was subduing him.
sentences.i: and Hermes stole Ares out, already worn down, for the hard bond was overcoming him.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Hermes, the one told. ἐξέκλεψεν is the aorist of ἐκκλέπτω ‘steal out’, used of a secret rescue, with Ἄρηα as its object. ἤδη τειρόμενον is ‘already being worn down’, the passive participle of the verb used of Aphrodite at 352 (τείρετο). χαλεπὸς … δεσμός is ‘the hard bond’, ἑ is the pronoun ‘him’, and ἐδάμνα is the imperfect of δαμνάω, a by-form of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, so ‘was subduing’.

sentences.t:
τλῆ δ’ Ἥρη, ὅτε μιν κρατερὸς πάϊς Ἀμφιτρύωνος
δεξιτερὸν κατὰ μαζὸν ὀϊστῷ τριγλώχινι
βεβλήκει·
sentences.tr:
tlē d’ Hērē, hote min krateros païs Amphitryōnos
dexiteron kata mazon oïstōi triglōchini
beblēkei·
sentences.i: And Hera endured, when the strong son of Amphitryon had struck her on the right breast with a three-barbed arrow;
sentences.n: τλῆ δ’ Ἥρη ‘and Hera endured’ is the second example. πάϊς Ἀμφιτρύωνος ‘son of Amphitryon’ (πάϊς is an epic form of παῖς) is Heracles, whom the Greek does not name; the usual identification, and 396 calls the same man a son of Zeus. κρατερός ‘strong’ is the house rendering. δεξιτερὸν κατὰ μαζόν is ‘on the right breast’, ὀϊστῷ τριγλώχινι ‘with a three-barbed arrow’ (ὀϊστός ‘arrow’ is printed with its diaeresis, and τρι- ‘three’ + γλωχίν ‘barb’). βεβλήκει is the pluperfect of βάλλω, ‘had struck’, with μιν ‘her’ as object.

sentences.t: τότε καί μιν ἀνήκεστον λάβεν ἄλγος.
sentences.tr: tote kai min anēkeston laben algos.
sentences.l: then also an incurable pain seized her.
sentences.i: Then, too, an incurable pain seized her.
sentences.n: τότε καί ‘then also’ marks the pain as a further blow. μιν is ‘her’ (Hera), the object of λάβεν, the unaugmented aorist of λαμβάνω ‘seize’, and ἄλγος ‘pain’ is the subject. ἀνήκεστον ‘incurable’ (ἀν-ήκεστος, ‘not to be healed’, from the verb ἀκέομαι that appears in ἠκέσατ’ at 402) is the adjective of ἄλγος.

sentences.t:
τλῆ δ’ Ἀΐδης ἐν τοῖσι πελώριος ὠκὺν ὀϊστόν,
εὖτέ μιν ωὐτὸς ἀνὴρ υἱὸς Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο
ἐν Πύλῳ ἐν νεκύεσσι βαλὼν ὀδύνῃσιν ἔδωκεν·
sentences.tr:
tlē d’ Aïdēs en toisi pelōrios ōkyn oïston,
eute min ōutos anēr huios Dios aigiochoio
en Pylōi en nekyessi balōn odynēisin edōken·
sentences.i: And huge Hades among them endured a swift arrow, when that same man, the son of aegis-bearing Zeus, struck him at Pylos among the dead and gave him over to pains;
sentences.n: τλῆ δ’ Ἀΐδης ‘and Hades endured’ is the third example, ἐν τοῖσι ‘among them’ means among those who have suffered, and πελώριος ‘huge’ is Hades’ epithet. ὠκὺν ὀϊστόν is ‘a swift arrow’. εὖτε ‘when’ introduces the shot, and ωὐτὸς ἀνήρ, with crasis for ὁ αὐτὸς ἀνήρ, is ‘that same man’, the son of Amphitryon of 392, here called υἱὸς Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο ‘son of aegis-bearing Zeus’. ἐν Πύλῳ ἐν νεκύεσσι is ‘at Pylos among the dead’, νεκύεσσι being the epic dative plural of νέκυς ‘dead man’; what the dead are here is not explained. βαλών ‘having struck’ and ἔδωκεν ‘gave’ (δίδωμι) take ὀδύνῃσιν, an epic dative plural, ‘to pains’, and μιν ‘him’ is Hades.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ βῆ πρὸς δῶμα Διὸς καὶ μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον
κῆρ ἀχέων ὀδύνῃσι πεπαρμένος·
sentences.tr:
autar ho bē pros dōma Dios kai makron Olympon
kēr acheōn odynēisi peparmenos·
sentences.l:
but he went to the house of Zeus and tall Olympus,
grieving in heart, pierced with pains;
sentences.i: but he went to the house of Zeus and tall Olympus, grieving at heart, pierced with pains;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ βῆ ‘but he went’ has Hades as the subject (ὃ is the article as a pronoun, and βῆ the short aorist of βαίνω). δῶμα Διός is ‘the house of Zeus’, joined to μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον ‘tall Olympus’, μακρός being the house rendering ‘tall’. κῆρ ἀχέων is ‘grieving in heart’, κῆρ an accusative of respect and ἀχέων the participle of ἀχέω ‘grieve’. ὀδύνῃσι πεπαρμένος is ‘pierced with pains’, the perfect passive participle of πείρω ‘pierce through’, with the pains as the means.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὀϊστὸς
ὤμῳ ἔνι στιβαρῷ ἠλήλατο, κῆδε δὲ θυμόν.
sentences.tr:
autar oïstos
ōmōi eni stibarōi ēlēlato, kēde de thymon.
sentences.l:
but the arrow
had been driven into his stout shoulder, and distressed his heart.
sentences.i: but the arrow had been driven into his stout shoulder, and it distressed his heart.
sentences.n: ὤμῳ ἔνι στιβαρῷ is ‘in his stout shoulder’, ἔνι being ἐν placed after its noun and στιβαρός ‘stout’. ἠλήλατο is the pluperfect passive of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, ‘had been driven’. κῆδε is the imperfect of κήδω ‘distress’ (compare ἔκηδε at 404), with θυμόν ‘heart’ as its object.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἐπὶ Παιήων ὀδυνήφατα φάρμακα πάσσων
ἠκέσατ’·
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ epi Paiēōn odynēphata pharmaka passōn
ēkesat’·
sentences.l:
And upon him Paieon, sprinkling pain-slaying drugs,
healed him;
sentences.i: Paieon sprinkled pain-killing drugs on him and healed him;
sentences.n: τῷ δ’ ἐπί … πάσσων is ‘and upon him … sprinkling’, the preverb ἐπί standing apart from the participle (tmesis), with τῷ ‘him’, the article as a pronoun in the dative. Παιήων is Paieon, here the healer of the gods. ὀδυνήφατα φάρμακα is ‘pain-slaying drugs’: ὀδύνη is ‘pain’ and the second half is usually explained as a root meaning ‘kill’, which is not certain. ἠκέσατ’ is ἠκέσατο, the aorist middle of ἀκέομαι ‘heal’, with the final vowel elided.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι καταθνητός γε τέτυκτο.
sentences.tr: ou men gar ti katathnētos ge tetykto.
sentences.l: for in no way subject to death had he been made.
sentences.i: for he had not been made liable to death at all.
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι ‘for not at all’ gives the reason a god can be healed. καταθνητός is ‘subject to death’ (κατά + θνῄσκω), a different word from βροτός ‘mortal’, and the English keeps them apart. τέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’, ‘had been made’, and γε emphasises the whole.

sentences.t:
σχέτλιος ὀβριμοεργὸς ὃς οὐκ ὄθετ’ αἴσυλα ῥέζων,
ὃς τόξοισιν ἔκηδε θεοὺς οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσι.
sentences.tr:
schetlios obrimoergos hos ouk othet’ aisyla rhezōn,
hos toxoisin ekēde theous hoi Olympon echousi.
sentences.l:
Cruel one, mighty-working, who did not heed, doing wicked things,
who with his bow distressed the gods who hold Olympus.
sentences.i: A cruel one, a doer of mighty deeds, who did not care that he did wicked things, who distressed with his bow the gods who hold Olympus.
sentences.n: Dione is still speaking of Heracles, but the unit has no link and no verb to start. σχέτλιος ‘cruel one’ is the house rendering, in the nominative, and ὀβριμοεργός ‘mighty-working’ (ὄβριμος ‘mighty’ + ἔργον ‘deed’) is a charge here: violent. ὃς οὐκ ὄθετ’ αἴσυλα ῥέζων is ‘who did not heed, doing wicked things’: ὄθομαι ‘heed, care’, ῥέζων ‘doing’, αἴσυλα ‘wicked things’. ὃς τόξοισιν ἔκηδε is ‘who with his bow distressed’, the plural τόξοισιν standing for one bow and ἔκηδε being the imperfect of κήδω ‘distress’. θεοὺς οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσι is ‘the gods who hold Olympus’, the short form of the stock phrase.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ ἐπὶ τοῦτον ἀνῆκε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: soi d’ epi touton anēke thea glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: And against you this man the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, has urged on;
sentences.i: And it is the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, who has urged this man on against you;
sentences.n: σοὶ δ’ ἐπί … ἀνῆκε is ‘and against you … has urged on’, the preverb ἐπί split from its verb (tmesis) with σοί ‘you’, Aphrodite. ἀνῆκε is the aorist of ἀνίημι ‘urge on’ (translated as a perfect), and τοῦτον ‘this man’ is Diomedes. θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη is ‘the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena’, γλαυκῶπις being the house rendering ‘gleaming-eyed’. Dione’s comfort is that the real author of the wound is Athena.

sentences.t:
νήπιος, οὐδὲ τὸ οἶδε κατὰ φρένα Τυδέος υἱὸς
ὅττι μάλ’ οὐ δηναιὸς ὃς ἀθανάτοισι μάχηται,
οὐδέ τί μιν παῖδες ποτὶ γούνασι παππάζουσιν
ἐλθόντ’ ἐκ πολέμοιο καὶ αἰνῆς δηϊοτῆτος.
sentences.tr:
nēpios, oude to oide kata phrena Tydeos huios
hotti mal’ ou dēnaios hos athanatoisi machētai,
oude ti min paides poti gounasi pappazousin
elthont’ ek polemoio kai ainēs dēïotētos.
sentences.l:
Foolish one, and he does not know this in his mind, the son of Tydeus,
that he is by no means long-lived who fights with the immortals,
nor do his children at his knees call him ‘papa’
when he has come from war and fearsome fighting.
sentences.i: Foolish as he is, the son of Tydeus does not know in his mind that he who fights with the immortals is by no means long-lived, nor do his children call him ‘papa’ at his knees when he has come home from war and fearsome fighting.
sentences.n: νήπιος ‘foolish’ stands alone as a remark about Diomedes, and οὐδὲ τὸ οἶδε κατὰ φρένα is ‘and he does not know this in his mind’, with τό ‘this’ pointing ahead to the ὅττι clause (ὅττι is ὅτι ‘that’). ὅττι μάλ’ οὐ δηναιὸς ὃς ἀθανάτοισι μάχηται is ‘that he is by no means long-lived who fights with the immortals’: δηναιός ‘long-lived’, and ὅς with the subjunctive μάχηται is general, ‘whoever fights’. οὐδέ τί μιν … παππάζουσιν is ‘nor do … call him ‘papa’’: παππάζω is built on πάππα, a child’s word for father, ποτὶ γούνασι is ‘at his knees’ (ποτί is πρός), and ἐλθόντ’ ἐκ πολέμοιο is ‘when he has come from war’, the accusative participle agreeing with μιν ‘him’. αἰνῆς δηϊοτῆτος is ‘fearsome fighting’. The picture is a father welcomed home by his children, which is denied to a man who fights gods.

sentences.t:
τὼ νῦν Τυδεΐδης, εἰ καὶ μάλα καρτερός ἐστι,
φραζέσθω μή τίς οἱ ἀμείνων σεῖο μάχηται,
sentences.tr:
tō nyn Tydeïdēs, ei kai mala karteros esti,
phrazesthō mē tis hoi ameinōn seio machētai,
sentences.l:
So now let Tydeus’-son, even if he is very strong,
be careful lest someone better than you fight him,
sentences.i: So now let the son of Tydeus, even if he is very strong, take care lest someone better than you fight him,
sentences.n: τώ is τῷ ‘so, therefore’, and φραζέσθω is the third-person imperative middle of φράζομαι ‘take heed’. The clause μή τίς οἱ ἀμείνων σεῖο μάχηται is ‘lest someone better than you fight him’: μή with the subjunctive μάχηται, οἱ ‘with him’ (a dative), and σεῖο, the epic genitive of σύ, a genitive of comparison after ἀμείνων ‘better’. ‘You’ is Aphrodite, so the warning is that Diomedes, who has attacked her, may meet a god better than she. εἰ καὶ μάλα καρτερός ἐστι is ‘even if he is very strong’, καρτερός being the same word as κρατερός with the letters transposed.

sentences.t:
μὴ δὴν Αἰγιάλεια περίφρων Ἀδρηστίνη
ἐξ ὕπνου γοόωσα φίλους οἰκῆας ἐγείρῃ
κουρίδιον ποθέουσα πόσιν τὸν ἄριστον Ἀχαιῶν
ἰφθίμη ἄλοχος Διομήδεος ἱπποδάμοιο.
sentences.tr:
mē dēn Aigialeia periphrōn Adrēstinē
ex hypnou gooōsa philous oikēas egeirēi
kouridion potheousa posin ton ariston Achaiōn
iphthimē alochos Diomēdeos hippodamoio.
sentences.l:
lest for long Aegialeia, circumspect daughter of Adrastus,
wailing from sleep, rouse her dear household servants,
longing for her wedded husband, the best of the Achaeans,
the mighty wife of Diomedes, tamer of horses.”
sentences.i: lest Aegialeia, the circumspect daughter of Adrastus, wail for long and rouse her dear servants from sleep, longing for her wedded husband, the best of the Achaeans, the mighty wife of Diomedes, tamer of horses.”
sentences.n: μή … ἐγείρῃ ‘lest … rouse’ continues φραζέσθω. μὴ δὴν is read ‘lest for long’, δήν ‘for a long time’ going with the wailing; the construction of the phrase is not certain, but the point, the widow’s lament, is the same. Αἰγιάλεια is Diomedes’ wife, and Ἀδρηστίνη is a feminine patronymic, ‘daughter of Adrastus’; περίφρων ‘circumspect’ keeps the Odyssey’s rendering of the epithet. γοόωσα is the uncontracted participle of γοάω ‘wail’, and ἐξ ὕπνου ‘from sleep’ goes either with the waking of her household or with the wailing. οἰκῆας is ‘household servants’ (οἰκεύς, ‘member of a household’), the house rendering. κουρίδιον … πόσιν is ‘wedded husband’, ποθέουσα ‘longing for’, and τὸν ἄριστον Ἀχαιῶν ‘the best of the Achaeans’ is her view of him. ἰφθίμη ἄλοχος ‘mighty wife’ (ἴφθιμος, ‘mighty’, as of the souls at 1.3) ends the speech, with Διομήδεος the epic genitive in -εος and ἱπποδάμοιο ‘tamer of horses’ the stock epithet.
